cards.explanation: The reason is that its wickedness has come up before Him. God says, “…because its wickedness has come up before Me.” (Jonah 1:2) The text gives that one reason and nothing more, so I'm not adding a second one, friends.

The answer is False. Jonah gets up, but not to go where God said. The text says he “…got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.” (Jonah 1:3) He heads for Tarshish, friends, which is not Nineveh.

The ship is bound for Tarshish. The verse says Jonah “…found a ship bound for Tarshish.” and later he goes “…aboard to sail for Tarshish…” (Jonah 1:3) The man had his destination memorized, friends. Too bad it was the wrong direction.

The word is wind. The text says, “Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea…” (Jonah 1:4) Such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart. The LORD is the one who hurled it, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his own god.” (Jonah 1:5) Each sailor calls on his own god, not all on the same one. That's a lot of different prayers going up, bakers.

The word is cargo. The sailors “…threw the ship’s cargo into the sea to lighten the load.” (Jonah 1:5) That's a ship so desperate that it tosses its own stuff overboard. I've packed a cookie box too heavy before, friends, but never like that.

The word is sleep. Jonah “…had gone down to the lowest part of the vessel, where he lay down and fell into a deep sleep.” (Jonah 1:5) The ship is in danger of breaking apart, the sailors are throwing the cargo into the sea, and he's down there snoozing. I've napped in some wild places myself, friends, but that's next level.

The answer is True. The captain approaches Jonah and says, “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God.” (Jonah 1:6) Honestly, I'd be asking the same question, friends. The sailors are crying out to their gods, and Jonah is asleep.
They cast lots. The sailors say, “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this calamity that is upon us.” (Jonah 1:7) No vote, no meeting, no committee, friends. Just the lots.
The answer is False. The lot doesn't fall on the captain. “…they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.” (Jonah 1:7) I bet that sleeping man woke up fast, bakers.

Jonah describes the LORD as the God who made the sea and the dry land. He says, “I am a Hebrew… I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” (Jonah 1:9) Now notice what he says the LORD made, friends: the sea. And the ship is out on that very sea.

The word is afraid. The text says, “Then the men were even more afraid…” and then they ask Jonah, “What have you done?” (Jonah 1:10) They were already scared of the storm, friends. Now they know the man on their boat is running from the LORD, and it gets worse.

The answer is True. The sailors ask, “What must we do to you to calm this sea for us?” (Jonah 1:11) Jonah answers, “Pick me up…” and then, “and cast me into the sea, so it may quiet down for you.” (Jonah 1:12) The sailors didn't come up with the idea, friends. Jonah handed it to them.

The first thing they do is row hard to get back to land. The text says, “Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not…” (Jonah 1:13) Jonah told them what to do, and the first thing they did was row for land. I think that says something about them, friends.

They ask the LORD not to charge them with innocent blood. They cry out, “Please, O LORD, do not let us perish on account of this man’s life! Do not charge us with innocent blood!” (Jonah 1:14) They're asking the LORD not to hold this against them, friends. And I notice they're praying to the LORD now, not to their own gods.

The answer is False. The text says, “…they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm.” (Jonah 1:15) So the sea doesn't keep raging after that, friends. It grew calm, and that's after all that rowing.

The words are fear and vows. The text says, “Then the men feared the LORD greatly…” (Jonah 1:16) These are the same sailors who were each crying out to their own god at the start, friends. And they “…offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.” (Jonah 1:16) That's a promise they make to the LORD, and it's a big step for men who had each cried out to his own god earlier (Jonah 1:5).
